body_markdown:
“Spicy-boy turbomonkey.” “Full chihuahua.” ** “An utterly ridiculous pop rock.” ** These are a few of the phrases coined by our editorial staff when we spent a day at Barber Motorsports Park with the[2023 GR Corolla (specifically, the Morizo Edition](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/track-tested-honda-civic-type-r-vs-toyota-gr-corolla-morizo/) ). Three and a half years have passed, and the wonderful people who designed this riotous three-cylinder hatchback have not left well enough alone. We got chassis and aero tweaks (2024), an[automatic transmission](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2025-toyota-gr-corolla-first-drive-automatic-for-the-people/) (2025),[more power for the base car, plus more chassis upgrades](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2026-gr-corolla-toyotas-ever-evolving-hot-hatch/) (2026), and most recently[a new model with the most intense, track-focused upgrades yet](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2026-toyota-grmn-corolla-pictures-specs/) . That version wears the hallowed letters GRMN, which stand for Gazoo Racing Masters of Nürburgring, a track that’s central to its story and to that of Gazoo Racing. As of last week, we’ve had a chance to drive it on track, and even after a brief stint, it’s clear that Toyota’s mad smile machine has gotten even more fun.


After five years of tutelage under Toyota’s late chief test driver[Hiromu Naruse](https://toyotagazooracing.com/nurburgring/contents/story/chapter1/) , Toyota CEO Akio Toyoda started racing (using a pseudonym) at the 24 Hours of Nürburgring in 2007. (He returned in 2009, 2014, 2016, and 2019, as well.) Since 2009, Toyota has used the GRMN badge to designate high-performance, limited-edition versions of various models for its home market in Japan. Toyoda’s pseudonym, Morizo, now graces the other high-performance version of the GR Corolla.


Toyota


Toyota


Toyota


Toyota


Though it is lighter, stiffer, and offers more oomph than the base GR Corolla, the GRMN was not born of a desire to chase statistics. “Morizo challenged us to create not simply a faster car,” says Naoyuki Sakamoto, its chief engineer, “but a car that gives the driver the confidence to keep pushing, even under the extreme conditions of the Nürburgring.” Learnings from the hydrogen-powered GR Corolla that competes in Japan’s endurance road racing series, Super Taikyu, extensively shaped the GRMN’s aerodynamic package, which includes a carbon-fiber hood with a unique center duct, new front side spoilers, carbon-fiber front fenders with unique ducts, and a rear wing with five settings.


Toyota


The GRMN, along with 2025-and-newer GR Corollas, uses 45.6 more feet of structural adhesive for a stiffer body. Engine torque is up by 7 lb-ft, to 302, between 4000 and 4600 rpm. A GRMN-specific intercooler cooling system draws water from a gallon-sized tank in the rear, next to the battery, and sprays it on the intercooler for up to 150 seconds to reduce intake air temperature by 14 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit. The twin-tube shocks of the base GR-rolla have been swapped for monotube units, which are inverted at the front of the car. The GRMN is limited to 730 units globally (“primarily for North America, Japan, and Australia” per the release, priced at $65,655. The base car, for comparison, is $41,815.


## Specs: 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla


- **Price:** $65,655 (base)
- **Powertrain:** 1.6-liter turbocharged DOHC inline-three, six-speed manual
- **Output:** 300 hp at 6500 rpm, 302 lb-ft at 3250—4600 rpm
- **Layout:** All-wheel-drive, four-door, two-passenger subcompact hatchback
- **Weight:** 3218.7 pounds
- **EPA Fuel Economy:** 21/28/24mpg (city/hwy/combined)
- **0–60 mph:** TBA
- **Competition:** Honda Civic Type R, Volkswagen Golf R


Toyota


Toyota


Thanks to the deletion of the rear seats, the GRMN weighs 66 pounds less than the regular GR ‘rolla.


To see what this all adds up to, we spent some time behind the wheel and riding shotgun in the GRMN Corolla at Eagles Canyon Raceway near Decatur, Texas. The track is 2.7 miles long with 16 turns and 150 feet of elevation change. For this event, Toyota put a chicane in the back stretch and instructed us to pass through pit row every lap, decisions that limited the theoretical top speed per lap and helped keep the drivetrain cooler. All cars were set to Track Mode, which operates differently as of the 2025 model year: For the first two model years, Track Mode instructs the GR-Four system to split torque front/rear in a fixed, 50:50 ratio. For 2025 and newer cars, Track Mode is a variable mode that splits torque in different ratios (ranging from 60:40 to 30:70 front/rear) depending on driver inputs, the state of the vehicle, and the demands of the track.


Like the Morizo Edition, the GRMN comes only with a close-ratio manual transmission.


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


To familiarize myself with the track, I hopped into an automatic-transmission, regular GR Corolla for a few laps. When I swapped into the GRMN, I immediately noticed a difference. The GRMN uses a much more aggressive tire—the street/track Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 vs. the Pilot Sport 4S summer—and the monotube shocks are much stiffer. I didn’t get to test how harsh the suspension/tire package is on the street, but on the track, they clarify feedback from the car significantly.


As I pushed the car harder and harder, under enthusiastic instruction from a pro in the right seat, I realized the car could handle much more power application than I thought it could, even when the wheels weren’t perfectly straight. Even as the tires started talking louder and louder, whether under acceleration or braking, the two Torsen LSDs and the clutched center driveline coupler shuffled power to help the car scramble out of every situation with its nose pointed in the right direction, the little three-cylinder snorting and snarling away. (According to Toyota, the system shifts from front- to rear-focused power at turn-in, maintains that rear bias through mid-corner, and at corner exit shifts power back toward the front.)


Toyota


Toyota


Toyota


The AWD system gave me the confidence to push the car harder and experience more of what the car could do—in a rear-wheel-drive car, I would have had a lower comfort threshold. The GRMN forgave my mistakes, and rewarded me by gobbling up power gleefully when I fed it at the right moment, and nudging its blunt nose right or left under light throttle/brake inputs. The short wheelbase helped, too, by making rotation and understeer easier to detect than in a larger car. Both the brakes and the shifter were predictable and intuitive: The brake pedal is linear and never grabby, and the pleasantly clunky shifter is easy to operate without looking, thanks to notchy gates and fairly short throws.


For a car that represents an already sporty car refined by highly experienced drivers who are sensitive to every nuance, the GRMN is an absolute hoot to drive in the hands of a beginner. Your author is still a novice when it comes to track driving, but I had so much fun in this car—and I walked away a slightly better driver than I was before. The GRMN may be the most extreme GR Corolla yet, but like the other versions, it will put a smile on the faces of both beginners and advanced drivers alike. We’re glad this car exists.


## 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla


**Highs:** Remarkably forgiving and fun on-track.
**Lows:** The hardest-core, limited-edition Corolla doesn’t come cheap.
**Summary:** A spendy, track-day version of a special, smile-inducing car.
